paragraphs.heading: A flowering of learning
paragraphs.text: The Islamic Golden Age was a time of cultural flowering in Islamic history, usually dated from the 8th to the 14th century. It is generally taken to start under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786–809), when the House of Wisdom was set up in Baghdad, then one of the largest cities in the world. This institution drew scholars from all over the Muslim world to put the classical learning of the known world into Arabic. Learning thrived beyond Baghdad too, in cities such as Cairo, Córdoba, Damascus, Samarkand and Fez, and later in Nasrid Granada.

paragraphs.heading: When did it end
paragraphs.text: Its end is usually placed in 1258, when the Mongols invaded, besieged Baghdad and brought down the Abbasid caliphate. Some scholars stretch it to about 1350 to take in the Timurid Renaissance. Others carry it into the 15th century to include the court of Granada, or even the 16th, with the rise of the Islamic gunpowder empires. There is no single agreed definition, and the span changes depending on whether the focus is culture or military success.

paragraphs.heading: Translating the ancients
paragraphs.text: The age is thought to have begun with a huge effort, in the eighth and ninth centuries, to gather and translate the ancient sciences of the Greeks. Muslims of the time were keen to absorb the scientific knowledge of the peoples they had conquered. Works by Galen, Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, Ptolemy and Archimedes were among those translated, out of Greek, Syriac, Middle Persian and Sanskrit and into Arabic and Syriac. Some of these texts, which might otherwise have been lost, were later passed on into Hebrew and Latin.

paragraphs.heading: Who did the work
paragraphs.text: Many translators were Christians, especially of the Church of the East, who turned Greek philosophy and science first into Syriac and then into Arabic. The House of Wisdom was led by the Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq, and for a long time the caliphs' personal doctors were often Assyrian Christians, among them the Bukhtishu family. Persians also made up a notably large share of the scientists of the period. The empire backed scholars heavily, and top translators such as Hunayn are estimated to have earned what professional athletes earn today.

paragraphs.heading: Original science
paragraphs.text: After the translation era came two centuries of striking original thinking, lasting from the late ninth century to the late eleventh, often called the golden age of Islamic science. The period after it is conventionally known as the 'age of decline'. Since the nineteenth century, this story of decline has become the favoured framework in general scholarship.

paragraphs.heading: The power of paper
paragraphs.text: Paper reached Muslim lands from China in the eighth century, mass-produced in Samarkand and Khorasan, and arrived in Al-Andalus in the 10th century. It was easier to make than parchment, cracked less than papyrus, and soaked up ink so that writing was hard to rub out, which suited record-keeping. Islamic papermakers used assembly-line methods to copy manuscripts by hand, turning out editions larger than any in Europe for centuries. Together with a new, easier writing system, this meant that, probably for the first time, a person could live solely by writing and selling books.

paragraphs.heading: Faith and knowledge
paragraphs.text: Religion may have helped drive this search for knowledge. Quranic teachings that value education and stress learning may have pushed Muslims of the age to study and to build up science. The central place of scripture made education a pillar of Islam, and a saying attributed to Muhammad holds that seeking knowledge is a duty for every Muslim.
